Scripture means sacred writing — text that a group of religious believers considers holy, divinely inspired, and carrying the highest spiritual authority. It is not just any old religious book. The defining quality of scripture is that the people who follow it believe the words come from God, a divine being, or a higher spiritual source — not merely from a human author's imagination or opinion. This is what separates scripture from other religious literature like sermons, commentaries, or spiritual self-help books: scripture is believed to be revealed, not invented.
The Two Main Ways the Word Is Used

The word "scripture" works at two levels, one broad and one specific.

1. The broad, general sense

In this sense, "scripture" refers to the sacred text(s) of any religion. Every major religion has its own scripture — writing it holds as divinely authoritative. The Bible is the scripture of Christianity. The Quran is the scripture of Islam. The Torah (or the larger Tanakh) is the scripture of Judaism. The Vedas, Upanishads, and Bhagavad Gita are among the scriptures of Hinduism. The Tripitaka is the scripture of Buddhism. The Guru Granth Sahib is the scripture of Sikhism.

When someone says "Hindu scripture teaches that the soul is eternal" or "Islamic scripture forbids certain foods," they are using the word in this broad sense — referring to whatever that religion's sacred text happens to be.

2. The specific, Christian sense

In everyday English, especially in Western contexts, "scripture" (and especially "the Scriptures" or "Holy Scripture") very often refers specifically to the Bible. This is so common that if someone says "Scripture says we should forgive our enemies" without specifying any religion, most English speakers will understand they mean the Bible. This narrower meaning comes from centuries of Christian usage in which the Bible was treated as the scripture — the definitive word of God.
Singular vs. Plural — a Subtle but Important Distinction

You will hear the word used in both forms, and they carry slightly different feelings:

  • "Scripture" (singular, no article, like "Scripture says..." or "according to Scripture") treats the entire sacred text as one unified whole — one body of divine truth. It feels solemn and authoritative, like referring to the text almost as a living voice.
  • "The scriptures" (plural) refers to the individual books, chapters, or texts that make up the collection. It draws attention to the fact that the Bible (or any religion's sacred texts) is actually a collection of many separate writings — the scriptures of the Hebrew prophets, the scriptures of the New Testament, etc.
  • "A scripture" means a single passage or verse from a sacred text. For example, "She recited a scripture from memory" means she quoted one passage.

Both singular and plural are correct and common. The plural feels a little more academic or historical; the singular feels more devotional.
What Makes Something "Scripture" and Not Just a Religious Book?

This is an important distinction. Not every book about religion is scripture. The key qualities are:

  • Believed to be divinely inspired or revealed: The religious community holds that God (or a divine force) guided the writing, spoke through the author, or directly delivered the text. This is what gives it ultimate authority.
  • Used as the foundational source of religious law, ethics, and belief: Communities turn to scripture to settle moral questions, guide worship, and define doctrine.
  • Treated with deep reverence: Scriptures are not casually tossed aside. They are studied carefully, recited in worship, memorized, and sometimes considered so sacred that they must be handled with care.

By contrast:

  • A pastor's sermon is based on scripture, but is not scripture itself.
  • A theology textbook explains scripture, but is not scripture.
  • A saint's letters or a pope's declarations may carry religious weight, but are generally not considered scripture in the same sense.
The Tone and Weight the Word Carries

"Scripture" is a formal, serious, and reverent word. When someone uses it, they are signaling that the text in question is not just important — it is considered the ultimate spiritual authority for that community. It carries a sense of finality and gravity. Saying "scripture teaches X" is a much stronger claim than saying "this religious book suggests X," because it implies the text's word is binding and divine.

The word can be used by believers speaking from within a faith ("Our scripture calls us to justice") or by scholars and outsiders describing a religion from the outside ("The Hindu scriptures are among the oldest religious texts ever written"). Both usages are correct — the word simply shifts slightly in tone depending on who is speaking.
Quick Summary to Anchor It All

Scripture = sacred, divinely-authoritative writing that a religious community holds as the word of God or a higher power. Used broadly, it covers the holy texts of any religion. Used specifically in English, it most often points to the Bible. It is not just any religious writing — it is the foundational, revealed text that a faith community turns to as the highest source of spiritual truth and guidance.
